transcripts.text:
**Liu Xiaobo (1955‑2017)** | Aspect | Details | |--------|---------| | **Early life & education** | Born in Changchun, Jilin Province. Studied literature at Jilin University (B.A., 1979) and later earned a Ph.D. in literary criticism from Beijing Normal University (1990). | | **Academic career** | Became a professor of literature and a respected literary critic. His scholarly work focused on modern Chinese poetry and the role of literature in society. | | **Turn to activism** | The 1989 Tiananmen Square protests were a turning point. Liu helped organize the student hunger strike and later wrote essays calling for political reform. After the crackdown, he was briefly detained and placed under surveillance. | | **Key initiatives** | 1. **“Democracy Wall” & “New Citizens’ Movement”** – In the early 1990s Liu co‑authored petitions demanding constitutional rights and the release of political prisoners.
2. **Charter 08 (2008)** – Liu was the principal drafter of this manifesto, signed by more than 300 Chinese intellectuals, calling for:
• Freedom of expression, assembly and religion
• An independent judiciary
• Multi‑party elections and the end of one‑party rule
• Protection of human rights as defined in the Universal Declaration of Human Rights. | | **Arrest & imprisonment** | - **December 2008:** Liu was arrested for “inciting subversion of state power” because of his role in Charter 08.
- **December 2009:** He was sentenced to 11 years in prison after a closed‑door trial. While incarcerated he continued to write essays and correspond with family and supporters, often smuggled out. | | **Nobel Peace Prize (2010)** | - **Awarded:** 10 October 2010, while Liu was still in prison.
- **Citation (paraphrased):** “For his long and non‑violent struggle for fundamental human rights in China.”
- **Why the Committee chose him:**
• **Non‑violent advocacy:** Liu’s work emphasized peaceful, intellectual protest rather than armed resistance.
• **Universal values:** His call for democracy, rule of law, and respect for human rights resonated with the Nobel Committee’s definition of “peace” as the promotion of justice and human dignity.
• **Symbolic impact:** Awarding Liu highlighted the plight of political prisoners worldwide and drew global attention to the lack of civil liberties in China. | | **After the award** | - The Chinese government rejected the prize, barred Liu from traveling to Oslo, and placed his family under tight surveillance.
- International leaders, human‑rights NGOs, and many Nobel laureates publicly supported Liu and called for his release. | | **Later years & death** | - Liu remained in prison until he died of liver cancer on 13 July 2017, after being denied timely medical treatment.
- His death sparked renewed calls for China to respect the rights of prisoners and to allow independent medical care. | | **Legacy** | - **Charter 08** continues to inspire Chinese dissidents and reformers.
- Liu is remembered as a moral conscience of modern China, a scholar who risked his freedom for universal human rights.
- The Nobel Peace Prize to a prisoner in an authoritarian state set a precedent for using the award as a platform for political and humanitarian advocacy. | ### In short Liu Xiaobo was a Chinese literary scholar turned human‑rights activist who, through essays, petitions, and the landmark Charter 08, championed non‑violent democratic reform in China. The Nobel Committee honored him in 2010 because his peaceful, intellectual struggle embodied the spirit of the Peace Prize—advancing fundamental human rights and the rule of law, even at great personal cost. His award brought worldwide attention to China’s suppression of dissent and cemented his status as a global symbol of peaceful resistance.
